title: Failover Ethos and Sales Talkbook
content:
Purpose:
This note is a compact talkbook for GTM + sales & solutions to explain Redwood's approach to graceful degradation, multi-region failover, and customer-facing transparency. It pairs practical comms scripts with competitive differentiators and a short set of realistic promises we can make to customers without over-committing.

High-level positioning (30s elevator):
- We design inference so your product stays useful even when infrastructure is stressed — by routing traffic, degrading features in predictable ways, and providing clear fallbacks that preserve core UX.
- Customers get a single control-plane across hosted, dedicated and private deployments so rollback and policy enforcement remain consistent.

Core principles (what to emphasize in demo / pitch):
- Predictable degradation: We expose graded-fallback policies (reduced context, lightweight quantized variants, regional routing) so product owners can choose the UX tradeoff they prefer.
- Observable impact: dashboards show exactly what percentage of requests hit fallbacks, the delta in latency/cost/quality, and token consumption.
- Safe defaults: reasonable conservative fallback rules out-of-the-box; strong controls for customers that require stricter degradation behavior.

What we will (and won't) promise:
- Commit: 'We will not silently change behavior — you'll have visibility and policy hooks to control fallback thresholds.'
- Commit: 'We will provide automated regional failover with traffic steering and a documented incident playbook.'
- Avoid: hard SLAs on output quality under degraded modes. Do not promise identical model outputs across variant fallbacks.

Talk tracks by audience:
- Developer/Engineer: focus on API compatibility, deterministic fallback hooks, SDK flags for feature toggles, and debug traces for degraded requests.
- Platform/Infra: emphasize routing, capacity tiers, canary rollouts and the ability to pin model variants per route.
- Security/Legal: highlight audit logs, private deployments, and explicit policy controls that prevent cross-tenant fallback exposure.
- Executive/Customer Execs: frame in terms of business continuity — what remains available (core flows), time-to-failover, and cost transparency.

Incident narrative templates (short):
1) Minor regional spike (developer-facing):
- Subject: "Partial regional latency — our mitigation steps"
- Body points: what happened, percentage of affected traffic, immediate fallback activated (quantized variant + region steer), customer impact (reduced latency, possible quality change), next steps and ETA for resolution.

2) Progressive capacity constraint (enterprise):
- Subject: "Traffic surge — temporary degraded mode enabled"
- Body: clear timeline of decision, why fallback chosen, how we measured quality delta, rollback criteria, how to opt-out of automatic fallback.

Suggested phrasing (trust language):
- Use verbs that signal transparency: "We observed", "We routed", "We mitigated", "We prioritized".
- Avoid absolutes about fidelity: "higher probability of unchanged outputs" vs "identical outputs".
- Reassuring close: "You can opt to disable automatic fallback and we'll support a manual escalation path."

Competitive differentiation notes:
- Competitor A: often touts 'always-on' claims but lacks per-request visibility and ties fallbacks to opaque autoscaling. Lead with our transparency and per-route fallback logs.
- Competitor B: strong regional presence but limited private deployment parity. Lead with the unified control plane across hosted/dedicated/private.
- Competitor C: cheaper single-model fallbacks; called out for introducing quality regressions without telemetry. Lead with our quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to eval sets.

Practical artifacts to show in demos:
- Live dashboard: 'fallback rate', median latency before/after fallback, token-cost delta, and per-route impact heatmap.
- Incident timeline: quick mock showing decisions and rollback path.
- Email template generator: prefilled messaging for affected customers, segmented by SLA tier.

Quick sample email (concise):
- Subject: "[Status] Temporary performance mitigation active — what to expect"
- Body: "We observed elevated latency in region X affecting ~8% of requests. To preserve core functionality we temporarily routed affected traffic to a lower-latency variant. You may notice slightly different outputs for long-context prompts. No data was exposed, and our rollback criteria are in place. We're monitoring and will update at hh:mm. For opt-out, contact your technical lead or open JIRA-OPS-927."

Metrics to show customers post-incident:
- % requests served by fallback by hour
- Median p95 latency pre/post fallback
- Token cost delta (%) for affected cohort
- Quality regression score on a canonical prompt set

Open questions for product and SRE:
- Which fallback policies should be exposed in the default tenant plan vs enterprise only?
- Can we commit to storing per-request fallback flags for 30d for audits?
- Runbook: who owns the outbound customer comms vs CS for enterprise incidents?

Next steps (GT M):
- Iterate with product to capture 3 canned demo stories and corresponding telemetry screenshots.
- Build short playbook cards for AE, SE, CSM audiences (one-pagers).
- Align legal on acceptable wording for "degraded quality" statements.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Consider a small "degradation badge" UI element apps can show to end users when fallback is active.
- Explore a customer opt-in to receive real-time webhook events when fallbacks trigger.

End."
